cur:monumental-sma-deesis.summary: Three standing, haloed figures are painted against a pale ground: at the centre the frontal figure of Christ holding a book, flanked by figures who turn towards him in intercession. This grouping, later called the Deesis, became one of the central images of Byzantine prayer.
facts: Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum preserves wall paintings from the 6th to the late 8th century; buried after an earthquake in 847, it was rediscovered only in 1900.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Byzantine frescos in Santa Maria Antiqua (Rome)

cur:monumental-sma-deesis.notes: Commons identifies the painting as a Deesis of John VII's time; the paint surface is damaged, and the identity of the flanking figures cannot be confirmed from the photograph.

cur:objects-easby-cross.summary: In the upper panel of the shaft Christ sits in majesty, haloed and holding a book, flanked by angels; below, haloed busts of the apostles are stacked in arched compartments, turning toward one another as if in conversation. The faces, soft and individual, show the influence of Late Antique and Carolingian models on Northumbrian sculptors. The cross gathered the apostolic Church around its Lord.
facts: Wikipedia records that four fragments survive; three were reused in the late 12th century in rebuilding St Agatha's Church, Easby, while the fragment with Christ in Majesty was recovered from a nearby field wall before 1869 and sold to the V&A in 1931.
Unusually, the stone is not local: it matches sandstone from the Aislaby quarries near Whitby, nearly 60 miles away.
cur:objects-easby-cross.notes: Image shows the upper part of the shaft (Christ in Majesty and apostles), not the whole reconstruction.

wga:zearly/1/2mural/5vialati/latina8.summary: Within an arched niche, Christ in a white pallium stands at the head of a great crowd, stretching out his hand with a slender rod toward a small temple-like tomb at the top of a flight of steps. The packed ranks of witnesses, continuing onto the adjoining wall, give this Raising of Lazarus an unusual sense of public drama. In a burial chamber, the scene proclaimed Christ's power over death and the hope of resurrection for those laid to rest there.
facts: The Via Latina catacomb (Via Dino Compagni) was a private underground cemetery, discovered by chance during building work in the mid-1950s; it was in use for only about fifty years, from the early 4th century to around 350–360.
Its paintings mix Christian and pagan subjects, suggesting that not all the families buried there had become Christian, which has led scholars to call it a 'picture gallery of the 4th century'.
The Web Gallery of Art notes that the small temple-like building (aedicula) stands as a metaphor for the grave of Lazarus, opposite the figure of Christ commanding him to rise.

wga:zearly/1/2mural/5vialati/latina8.notes: The specific cubiculum was not confirmed. A faint figure and a column painted higher up in the lunette were not identified and are not described.
